title: UK Clearing 2026: Questions Worth Asking Before You Say Yes
description: Considering Falmouth University through Clearing 2026? Ask about teaching, disability support, accommodation, location, finance and next steps.
standfirst: Considering Falmouth University through Clearing 2026? These questions can help you think beyond the offer itself and check what studying, living and getting support there could actually look like.
imageAlt: Colourful graphic reading Clearing: Questions worth asking before you say yes, with a United Kingdom flag icon.
caption: Questions worth asking before you accept a university place through Clearing.
bodyHtml:
Clearing can get very “there’s a place — say yes!” very quickly.

But getting an offer and finding somewhere that actually works for you are not quite the same thing.

Before you commit, it is worth asking what studying and living there might actually look like — especially if accessibility, accommodation, routine or support will affect your day-to-day life.

You do not need to ask everything. You just need enough information to make a decision that feels informed rather than rushed.

For Falmouth University, information for Clearing can be found here: https://www.falmouth.ac.uk/study/clearing.

Teaching: How is the course actually taught?

A course can sound perfect on a website and still feel very different once you are there.

Ask what a typical week looks like. Think about contact hours, group work, presentations, practical work, independent study and how you will be assessed.

If predictability matters to you, it is also worth asking how timetables usually work and how much they can change.

Support: How are reasonable adjustments and disability support arranged?

Reasonable adjustments are changes that can help reduce disability-related barriers to studying.

You can ask how support is arranged, who you would need to contact and whether you can start discussing your needs before you arrive.

You do not have to explain your whole medical history during a Clearing call just to find out how the process works.

Living: Can the available accommodation meet your needs?

“Accommodation is available” does not always mean “the accommodation available will work for me”.

Think about noise, sensory needs, accessibility, bathroom facilities, cooking arrangements, flat size and how far you would be from teaching.

You may also want to ask about both university accommodation and private options nearby.

If where you live is going to affect how manageable university feels, it is worth asking about it before you decide.

Location: Where will you actually be studying?

This sounds obvious, but it can make a big difference.

Some courses are taught across different campuses or sites, so ask where most of your teaching will actually happen.

If you are looking at Falmouth University, for example, you might want to know whether your course is mainly based at Falmouth, Penryn or Woodlane.

Then think about the everyday journey: accommodation, buses, walking, shops, healthcare and any services you may rely on.

You are choosing somewhere to live as well as somewhere to study.

Finance: What support or funding might you need to arrange or update?

If you receive, or may be eligible for, Disabled Students’ Allowance (DSA), it is worth checking whether anything needs to be applied for or updated if your university or course changes.

You may also need to update Student Finance or contact university support services once your place is confirmed.

You do not need to sort all of this out during the call.

The useful question is simply: What do I need to do next?

What’s Next: What happens if you are offered a place?

If a university offers you a place through Clearing, ask what happens next.

  • How long do you have to decide?
  • What do you need to do through UCAS?
  • When can you apply for accommodation?
  • Is there anything you should complete before starting?

When everything is moving quickly, having those next steps written down can make the process much easier to manage.

Clearing is not only about finding a space

It is easy to treat Clearing as a race to find somewhere with places left.

But you are also choosing a course, an environment, a place to live and a university system you may be navigating for the next few years.

So yes, ask: “Can I get in?”

But also ask: “Can I see myself studying, living and being supported here?”

That second question might tell you much more!

Starting university in September 2026?

Building Identity Through Stories (BITS) is a creative research project exploring how storytelling, art, memes, sound and digital media might support SEND and neurodivergent students through the transition into university.

The project is interested in the parts of starting university that do not always fit neatly into an induction checklist: identity, belonging, uncertainty, finding your people and working out how university fits around who you are.

There will be creative workshops, reflective prompts and more transition-focused content coming soon!

Disclaimer: This is an independent informational post and is not official guidance from, endorsed by, or representative of Falmouth University. Clearing information can change, so please check UCAS and the relevant university’s official website for the latest information.

title: Finding Private Accommodation in Falmouth & Penryn: A Neurodivergent Guide
description: A practical guide to finding private accommodation in Falmouth and Penryn for neurodivergent, disabled and SEND students, from searching to signing.
standfirst: Looking for private student accommodation in Falmouth or Penryn? This guide covers where to search, what to check at viewings and what to confirm before you sign.
imageAlt: Student standing with luggage in a field beneath text reading “Finding Private Accommodation: A Neurodivergent Guide”, with Falmouth and Penryn named above.
bodyHtml:
Finding somewhere to live in Falmouth or Penryn can get stressful quickly. One minute you are browsing rooms. The next, you have ten tabs open, someone wants a guarantor, and a housemate is asking whether you can sign today.

If you are neurodivergent, disabled or have special educational needs and disabilities (SEND), the practical details can matter a lot: noise, who you live with, the journey to campus, bills, shared spaces and whether you have somewhere to properly switch off.

So, where should you look?

A quick note on links: We’ve included external websites and groups that might be useful. They’re independent from this website, so a link does not mean we endorse them. Check the details carefully before making any payments or commitments.

1. Start with Cornwall Studentpad

Cornwall Studentpad - https://www.cornwallstudentpad.co.uk/ is the official accommodation search platform for students at Falmouth University and the University of Exeter’s Cornwall campuses.

It includes student houses, individual rooms, flats and lodgings in Falmouth, Penryn and nearby areas.

If you are moving alone, FX Plus also provides support with finding housemates. Studentpad is a sensible first stop before opening several different property sites.

2. Check local Facebook groups

Facebook groups can turn up rooms that never reach the bigger property websites.

Useful groups include:

  • Falmouth Exeter Plus - Housemate Finder
  • Falmouth Private Student Accommodation
  • Falmouth & Penryn Student Accommodation: Find Housing & Flatmates
  • Private Accommodation to Rent in Cornwall
  • Houses to Rent in Cornwall
  • Need room to rent in Falmouth
  • Falmouth & Penryn Homeswaps
  • Falmouth/Penryn Accommodation & Spare Rooms

If you are joining an existing house, use the group to find out a little more before arranging a viewing. Ask whether the house is generally quiet or social, how often people have friends over, and how cleaning and shared spaces tend to work.

For informal listings, check who you are dealing with and verify the property and tenancy details before sending money.

3. Use Rightmove and other property sites

Rightmove - https://www.rightmove.co.uk and OnTheMarket - https://www.onthemarket.com/ are useful for rooms, flats and whole student houses.

Set your budget, move-in date, preferred area and furnished or unfurnished preference before you start scrolling. If you are searching alone, filter for individual rooms. It saves you from repeatedly opening five- or six-bedroom houses that need a complete group.

4. Consider private student halls

Private purpose-built student accommodation is another option. The Quarry and Carrick View, for example, offer en-suite rooms and studios.

Bills and Wi-Fi may be included, which can reduce the number of separate payments to manage each month. Compare that with the cost, location and amount of shared space before deciding.

Before you book a viewing

Pick three things that would make the biggest difference to everyday life.

That might be a quieter bedroom, fewer housemates, an en-suite bathroom, bills included, a straightforward journey to campus, or enough kitchen space for your usual routine.

Then check those things properly at the viewing.

Listen for traffic and noise from communal areas. Look at the bedroom light and storage. Check how many people share the kitchen and bathroom, and map the actual journey to campus rather than relying on the description in the advert.

Before you sign anything

The housing market can move quickly, but urgency is not a reason to sign a contract you do not understand.

Check:

  • total rent and deposit
  • tenancy dates
  • whether bills are included
  • guarantor requirements
  • who deals with repairs
  • whether the tenancy is joint or individual

If something is unclear, ask before signing or paying anything.

Quick FAQ

Can I find a room if I do not already have housemates?

Yes. Look for individual rooms in existing student houses, lodgings or studio accommodation. FX Plus also provides support with finding housemates.

Is Penryn too far from Falmouth University?

It depends on your campus and how you travel. Check the actual walking, bus or train journey from the property before deciding.

What if I need quieter accommodation?

Look beyond the word “quiet” in the advert. Check the road, bedroom position, number of housemates and distance from kitchens or shared areas. If your requirements relate to a disability or health condition, you can also speak with university accommodation or disability support services.

Before committing, check the property against the few things that matter most to your day-to-day routine. A room can look good online and still be the wrong setup once you are living there.

title: Is an Online Degree More Accessible for SEND and Neurodivergent Students?
description: Explore how online degrees may remove some barriers for SEND and neurodivergent students, while creating new challenges around structure and support.
standfirst: Online study can remove barriers such as travel and sensory overload, but it can also create new challenges around structure, digital systems and support. Here’s what to check before deciding whether an online course is more accessible for you.
imageAlt: Student working on a laptop at a table beneath text asking whether an online degree is more accessible for SEND and neurodivergent students.
bodyHtml:
Online degree can look like the more accessible option.

No commute. No packed lecture theatres. More control over noise, lighting and breaks. Maybe you can replay teaching instead of trying to process everything in real time.

For some students with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) and neurodivergent students, that can make a real difference. But online does not automatically mean accessible. It may remove some barriers while creating others.

Starting university is also a transition, whether you arrive on campus or log in from home. You are still learning new routines, new systems, new expectations and new ways of asking for support. The question is not only whether an online course looks accessible, but whether its design makes that transition easier to navigate.

The barriers can change

Online study may help if travel, sensory overload or busy campus environments take a lot of energy.

But it can also mean:

  • more independent organisation;
  • more screen time;
  • less external structure;
  • support that feels less visible;
  • more reliance on digital platforms; and
  • fewer casual opportunities to ask someone for help.

So the useful question is not: “Is online university more accessible?”

It is: “Is this online course more accessible for me?”

Check what “online” actually means

Before accepting an offer, find out how the course really works.

Ask:

  • Are lectures live, recorded or both?
  • Are there fixed attendance times?
  • How much group work is there?
  • Are presentations required?
  • How are exams and assessments delivered?
  • Are there any compulsory campus days or placements?

A course can be described as flexible while still expecting you to be online at specific times every week.

If you are considering Falmouth, its How You Study Online and Online Learning Support pages give a useful picture of how this works in practice. Online students have Academic Tutors for course-related support and dedicated Student Advisors who can help with things such as wellbeing, accessibility and navigating university support.

Ask how support actually works

“We support disabled students” sounds reassuring, but it does not tell you much about what will happen in practice.

Ask things like:

  • Can I get live captions or transcripts?
  • Are lectures recorded?
  • Can materials be provided in accessible formats?
  • Are alternative presentation arrangements possible?
  • Is specialist mentoring available remotely?
  • Who do I contact if an agreed adjustment is not happening?

At Falmouth, the Disability Support page explains how Individual Learning Plans (ILPs) work. An ILP can communicate recommended reasonable adjustments to your course team, and students can apply through My Falmouth.

If digital accessibility is important for you, it is also worth checking the Falmouth Learn accessibility statement. It explains features such as keyboard navigation, zoom up to 400% and compatibility with screen readers including JAWS, NVDA and VoiceOver, as well as known accessibility limitations.

That kind of information can help you work out whether the actual digital learning environment is likely to work with the tools and setup you use.

What about missing the campus experience?

Online students may miss some of the informal parts of university life — welcome events, societies, or simply meeting people between classes. That can affect how transition feels.

If peer connection matters to you, the Falmouth & Exeter Students’ Union Neurodiversity & Disability Society is one example of a student-led space for meeting people with similar experiences and finding community.

This is also part of my PhD project, Building Identity Through Stories (BITS), which explores how creative storytelling might support SEND and neurodivergent students during the transition into university.

As part of the project, I’ll also be hosting online creative workshops - https://bitsresearch.github.io/#upcoming-workshops, so students who are not regularly on campus can still take part, share experiences and connect with others in a low-pressure space.

Quick FAQ

Is online university easier for neurodivergent students?

  • Not necessarily. Some students benefit from flexibility and greater control over their environment, while others find reduced structure more difficult.

Can online students get reasonable adjustments?

  • Yes. What is reasonable will depend on your needs, the course and the barriers involved, so speak to the university’s disability service about how adjustments work online.

Can distance-learning students get DSA?

  • Eligible distance-learning students can receive Disabled Students’ Allowance (DSA). Eligibility rules vary, so check the guidance for where you normally live.

Should I contact disability support before starting university?

  • Yes. It can be especially useful if you already know you may need adjustments.

Disclaimer: This is an independent informational post and is not official guidance from, endorsed by, or representative of Falmouth University. Course delivery, support, reasonable adjustments and funding arrangements vary, so please check directly with the relevant university or official service.
